claims.quote: all of our stock markets and all of our portfolios and 401(k)s are partially built on borrowed Japanese money
claims.claim: US stock markets, investment portfolios and 401(k) balances are partially built on borrowed Japanese money [channelled through the yen carry trade].
claims.basis: The claim turns on the size of the yen carry trade, which has no agreed measurement basis: bank-based accounting and FX-swap notional accounting differ by more than an order of magnitude, and the word 'partially' is a hedge no single figure settles. Published estimates were not retrieved; research cut off by session limit.

claims.quote: That tweet got millions of views
claims.claim: An anonymous Japanese-language X post apologising to Western countries for measures the Bank of Japan was preparing got millions of views.
claims.basis: Requires reading view counts on a specific pseudonymous X post; the post was not located and X view metrics are not retrievable without an authenticated session. Research cut off by session limit.

claims.quote: no one really knows who this person is. The account goes by the name Yuto. It posts exclusively in Japanese
claims.claim: The viral X account making claims about Bank of Japan policy goes by the name 'Yuto', is of unknown identity, and posts exclusively in Japanese.
claims.basis: Identifying a pseudonymous account and confirming that every one of its posts is in Japanese needs the account itself; it was not located. Research cut off by session limit.

claims.quote: 12 days after that first post, they posted again
claims.claim: The same anonymous account posted its second viral message, about Japan's wealth returning to its homeland, 12 days after the first.
claims.basis: Needs timestamps on two specific posts from a pseudonymous account; not located. Research cut off by session limit.

claims.quote: increased their interest rates to levels that we haven't seen since 1995
claims.claim: Japan raised its interest rates in 2026 to levels not seen since 1995.
claims.basis: Needs the Bank of Japan's 2026 policy rate decisions and the historical path of the uncollateralized overnight call rate back to 1995; neither was retrieved. Research cut off by session limit.

claims.quote: Japan has more government debt relative to the size of its economy than any developed country in the world. Over 200% of GDP
claims.claim: Japan has more government debt relative to the size of its economy than any developed country, over 200% of GDP.
claims.label: confirmed
claims.basis: IMF DataMapper, general government gross debt as percent of GDP, 2026 projection: Japan 204.4, Italy 138.4, Greece 136.9, United States 125.8. Measurement basis matters: this is gross debt for the general government sector, and on a net basis Japan's ratio is roughly a third lower because the government's own holdings net out. https://www.imf.org/external/datamapper/api/v1/GGXWDG_NGDP/JPN/GRC/USA/ITA

claims.quote: Japan has more debt than Greece when Greece collapsed
claims.claim: Japan's government debt to GDP ratio is higher than Greece's was when Greece's debt crisis hit.
claims.label: confirmed
claims.basis: Same IMF series, general government gross debt as percent of GDP: Greece 175.1 (2011), 180.5 (2013), 182.8 (2014), against Japan 204.4 (2026). Greece's own all-time peak of 209.9 came in 2020, a decade after the collapse the claim refers to, so the comparison holds on the period named. https://www.imf.org/external/datamapper/api/v1/GGXWDG_NGDP/JPN/GRC/USA/ITA

claims.quote: They have more debt than any country that's ever hyper-inflated
claims.claim: Japan's debt to GDP ratio is higher than that of any country that has ever experienced hyperinflation.
claims.basis: Ill-posed as stated: hyperinflation destroys the denominator, so debt to GDP ratios for Weimar Germany, Zimbabwe or Venezuela at the moment of hyperinflation are either unmeasured or not comparable to a modern IMF series. No comparable dataset was retrieved; research cut off by session limit.

claims.quote: the land under the Imperial Palace in Tokyo was worth more than all the real estate in California
claims.claim: At the peak of Japan's 1980s bubble, the land under the Imperial Palace in Tokyo was worth more than all the real estate in California.
claims.label: plausible
claims.basis: Wikipedia's account of the Japanese asset price bubble states that 'the 1.15 square kilometer Tokyo Imperial Palace grounds were estimated to be worth more than the entire real estate value of California' at the peak. It is a bubble-era estimate that circulates in several variants (California, or all of Canada), and the underlying valuation was not traced to a primary appraisal, so it is consistent with the record rather than directly confirmed. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_asset_price_bubble

claims.quote: three decades of deflation. The price of stuff did not go up
claims.claim: After its early 1990s bubble burst, Japan experienced three decades of deflation during which prices did not rise.
claims.basis: Needs Japan's CPI history from 1990 to 2020 to establish how much of that period was outright deflation rather than very low positive inflation; the series was not retrieved. Research cut off by session limit.

claims.quote: the Bank of Japan lowered interest rates to zero, and basically left them there for 30 years
claims.claim: The Bank of Japan cut interest rates to zero after the bubble burst and left them there for about 30 years.
claims.basis: Needs the Bank of Japan's policy rate history, including the date zero interest rate policy began and the 2006 to 2008 interlude when the target was above zero; not retrieved. Research cut off by session limit.

claims.quote: The Bank of Japan itself holds about 48% of all Japanese government bonds
claims.claim: The Bank of Japan holds about 48% of all Japanese government bonds outstanding.
claims.label: confirmed
claims.basis: Japan Ministry of Finance, Breakdown by JGB and T-Bill Holders, March 2026 preliminary figures: Bank of Japan 485.4 trillion yen, 47.9% of JGBs. Measurement basis is decisive here: that 47.9% is JGBs excluding Treasury discount bills, and the same table puts the BOJ at 42.2% once T-Bills are included. https://www.mof.go.jp/english/policy/jgbs/publication/newsletter/jgb2026_07e.pdf

claims.quote: Japanese insurance companies hold another 20%, Japanese banks 14%, and the foreigners own less than 8%
claims.claim: Japanese insurance companies hold 20% of Japanese government bonds, Japanese banks 14%, and foreign investors less than 8%.
claims.label: plausible
claims.basis: Same MoF table, March 2026 preliminary, JGBs excluding T-Bills: insurance companies 155.3 trillion yen (15.3%), banks 149.7 trillion (14.8%), foreigners 82.0 trillion (8.1%). Banks match, the foreign share is fractionally above the stated 'less than 8%', and insurance is overstated by about 5 percentage points unless private pension funds (3.1%) are folded in, which gets to 18.4%. Including T-Bills moves foreigners to 13.7%, so the sub-8% figure only survives on the JGB-only basis. https://www.mof.go.jp/english/policy/jgbs/publication/newsletter/jgb2026_07e.pdf

claims.quote: Since 2004, the US money supply grew by about 280%
claims.claim: The US money supply has grown by about 280% since 2004.
claims.label: confirmed
claims.basis: FRED M2SL (M2, seasonally adjusted, billions of dollars): 6,081.3 in January 2004 and 23,218.0 in July 2026. 23,218.0 / 6,081.3 = 3.818, i.e. +281.8%, against the claimed 'about 280%'. Basis is M2 in nominal local currency, not real or per capita. https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/M2SL

claims.quote: Canada grew by 370% but Japan only grew by 90
claims.claim: Since 2004 Canada's money supply grew by 370% while Japan's grew by only 90%.
claims.label: confirmed
claims.basis: Canada, Bank of Canada series V41552796, M2 gross seasonally adjusted, millions of dollars: 604,836 in January 2004 and 2,840,155 in June 2026, = +369.6%. Japan, M2 average amounts outstanding: 681.7 trillion yen in January 2004 (FRED MYAGM2JPM189S) and 1,297.0 trillion yen in July 2026 (Bank of Japan Money Stock, preliminary figures for July 2026), = +90.2%. Both are broad money in nominal local currency, the same basis as the US figure in J14. https://www.bankofcanada.ca/valet/observations/V41552796/csv and https://www.boj.or.jp/en/statistics/money/ms/ms2607.pdf

claims.quote: That's estimated to be worth trillions of dollars of investments all around the world funded by borrowed Japanese money
claims.claim: The yen carry trade funds trillions of dollars of investments around the world.
claims.basis: Estimates of the carry trade's size span more than an order of magnitude depending on whether the measure is cross-border yen bank lending, yen-denominated securities positions, or FX swap notional. No published estimate was retrieved to fix the range; research cut off by session limit.

claims.quote: Japan became the world's biggest foreign holder of US government debt. Holding something like over a trillion dollars of US Treasuries

claims.quote: the yen is trading at about 160-ish yen per dollar
claims.claim: At the time the video was made [late July 2026] the yen was trading at about 160 per dollar.
claims.label: plausible
claims.basis: FRED DEXJPUS noon buying rates for the week the video was recorded: 163.01 on 21 July 2026, 163.08 on 22 July, 163.80 on 23 July, 163.71 on 24 and 27 July, 163.65 on 28 July, and a July high of 163.86 on 29 July. The July 2026 monthly average (FRED EXJPUS) was 162.33. '160-ish' is loose by about 3 yen in the direction that understates the move, and the same passage goes on to say the level is very close to 164, which only makes sense at the true 163. https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DEXJPUS

claims.quote: which is also the lowest level that it's been against the dollar in about 40 years
claims.claim: The yen's July 2026 level against the dollar was its weakest in about 40 years.
claims.label: confirmed
claims.basis: Computed over the full FRED DEXJPUS daily series: the weakest yen between January 1990 and December 2023 was 159.90 on 17 April 1990, and the weakest of 2024 was 161.73 on 10 July 2024, both stronger than July 2026's 163.86 on 29 July. The last dates weaker than that fall between mid-1986 (174.90 on 2 June 1986) and the end of the 1980s, so 'about 40 years' is right, and the July 2026 level also cleared the 2024 low that was itself reported as a 38-year low. https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DEXJPUS

claims.quote: Ronald Reagan was president and Nintendo had just come out

claims.quote: The 30-year bond is at about 4%

claims.quote: This is around -150,000 contracts. In dollar terms, it's roughly 11-12 billion dollars of bets against the yen

Research cut off by session limit.

claims.quote: it's paying about 4.7%

claims.quote: In 1998, the yen went up 15% in just 3 days

claims.claim: During the March 2020 COVID crash the yen strengthened while every other asset was being sold.
claims.label: misleading
claims.basis: FRED DEXJPUS shows the opposite during the crash itself. The yen did strengthen from 111.86 on 20 February 2020 to 102.52 on 9 March, but then reversed hard through the dollar funding squeeze: 105.64 on 16 March, 108.45 on 18 March, 110.08 on 19 March, 111.30 on 20 March, and 111.44 on 24 March, its weakest of the month. The equity low was 23 March, the day the yen was near its weakest, so during the worst of the sell-off the yen was sold alongside everything else. The kernel of truth is the late-February leg, which is not what 'March 2020, COVID crash' describes. https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DEXJPUS

claims.quote: the Bank of Japan increased interest rates by just a little, a quarter of 1%
claims.claim: In August 2024 the Bank of Japan increased interest rates by a quarter of one percent.
claims.label: plausible
claims.basis: Bank of Japan, 'Change in the Guideline for Money Market Operations', 31 July 2024: the Policy Board decided by a 7-2 vote to 'encourage the uncollateralized overnight call rate to remain at around 0.25 percent', with the new guideline 'effective from August 1, 2024'. So the resulting level was a quarter of 1% and it took effect in August, but the increase itself was about 15 basis points, from a target of around 0 to 0.1 percent, not 25. https://www.boj.or.jp/en/mopo/mpmdeci/mpr_2024/k240731a.pdf

claims.quote: in one day Japan's stock market went down 12%. The worst day since 1987
claims.claim: Japan's stock market fell 12% in one day in August 2024, its worst day since 1987.
claims.label: confirmed
claims.basis: FRED NIKKEI225 daily closes: 35,909.70 on 2 August 2024 to 31,458.42 on 5 August 2024, a fall of 12.40%. Ranking every daily change in that series, which starts 16 May 1949, the only larger single-day fall is 14.90% on 20 October 1987; the next worst are 11.41% (16 October 2008) and 10.55% (15 March 2011), both after 1987 and both smaller. Both halves of the claim hold. https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/NIKKEI225

claims.quote: the US stock market went down 3%
claims.claim: The US stock market fell 3% on the same day as Japan's 12% fall in August 2024.
claims.label: confirmed
claims.basis: FRED SP500 daily closes: 5,346.56 on 2 August 2024 to 5,186.33 on 5 August 2024, a fall of 3.00%, the same session as the Nikkei's 12.40% drop in J68. https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/SP500

claims.quote: the yen going up is not what causes these things to happen
claims.claim: A rising yen does not cause global market crises; the causation runs the other way, with a crisis triggering a carry trade unwind that pushes the yen up.
claims.basis: A causal interpretation of the episodes listed above rather than a discrete assertion a source could settle; the direction of causation between carry unwinds and crises is contested in the literature and is not rateable as stated.

claims.quote: deposit $100 with WeBull to grab your 12 free stocks
claims.claim: [Sponsor read] Depositing 100 dollars with Webull gets you 12 free stocks.
claims.basis: Needs Webull's promotion terms as of July 2026, including the deposit threshold, the holding period and what 'free stocks' actually means. Not retrieved; research cut off by session limit.

claims.quote: Japan has broken every rule of economics and still somehow got away with it
claims.claim: Japan has broken every rule of economics and got away with it.
claims.basis: Rhetorical characterisation, not a checkable assertion: no source can settle what 'every rule of economics' is or what counts as getting away with it.

claims.quote: they make arguably the best culture in the world
claims.claim: Japan makes arguably the best culture in the world.
claims.basis: Explicitly hedged aesthetic preference, not rateable.

claims.quote: That is partially why interest rates are expected to go up here in the US
claims.claim: US interest rates are expected to rise partly because Japan is stepping back as a buyer of US debt.
claims.basis: A forward-looking claim about rates that had not resolved at the time of labelling, and its attribution of cause is untestable in advance; predictions are not rateable.
